article.articleHeadline: Ebola outbreak 2026: With over 4,000 cases, Congo battles its deadliest surge as virus gets out of control
article.articleSummary: DRC Ebola outbreak 2026 tops 4,000 cases, the deadliest surge, with North Kivu and Ituri provinces hardest hit. Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) is caused by Ebolavirus; six species exist, with Zaire ebolavirus driving most DRC outbreaks and historically bearing the highest case fatality (roughly 25–90% depending on care). Early symptoms mimic malaria and typhoid, delaying diagnosis and enabling spread through households and health workers, with nosocomial and superspreading amplification. Response is hampered by armed conflict and weak health systems in eastern Congo, delaying ring vaccination and contact tracing. Containment hinges on rapid case detection, isolation, ring vaccination with Ervebo (rVSV-ZEBOV), point-of-care diagnostics like GeneXpert, and therapies REGN-EB3 and mAb114, supported by WHO and Africa CDC, alongside community engagement and safe burial practices.

article.articleHeadline: SARS-CoV-2, mpox, chikungunya, hantavirus, Ebola... Why are viral emergences multiplying?
article.articleSummary: Viral emergences are increasing due to climate warming, population movement, and intensive farming, creating a 'perfect storm' for spread. Since SARS-CoV-2, pathogens such as mpox, chikungunya, hantavirus, and Ebola have repeatedly shifted from animal reservoirs to humans. Mpox caused about 100,000 confirmed cases across more than 120 countries between 2022–2023, with France reporting over 4,000 cases, mostly in 2022. In 2025 France saw unusually high locally acquired chikungunya, with more than 800 autochthonous cases. In 2026, Andes hantavirus outbreaks were linked to the MV Hondius, and an Ebola flare occurred in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Viruses evolve rapidly via mutations, recombination, and reassortment, outpacing bacteria, and about 75% of emerging human viruses originate in animals (zoonoses).

article.articleHeadline: DRCongo: Cholera epidemic continues to rage in Kwilu province
article.articleSummary: Cholera outbreak in western Democratic Republic of the Congo's Kwilu province: 419 cases and 30 deaths since June, across four health zones (Bandundu, Kikongo, Mokala, Ipamu). Bandundu reports 212 cases and 14 deaths with over 198 recovered; Kikongo 166 cases and 8 deaths with over 100 recovered; Mokala and Ipamu remain active, with ongoing interventions. Unsafe Kasai River water identified as a key transmission factor. Water chlorination and targeted operations are underway in Piopio and Panu (Mokala) and Kinkole (Ipamu). The response is led by the central and Kwilu provincial governments, providing water treatment supplies, PPE for health workers, and disinfection equipment. Africa CDC notes a broader 2026 trend with over 33,000 total cases and 943 deaths nationwide. No new cases reported in Bandundu and Kikongo at present; Mokala and Ipamu still experiencing transmission.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in Ituri: Cancellation of the 2026 diocesan pilgrimage scheduled for Erira - ACP
article.articleSummary: On 9 August 2026, the Diocese of Mahagi-Nioka in Ituri, northeast Democratic Republic of Congo, cancelled the 2026 diocesan pilgrimage to the Erira sanctuary to curb Ebola virus disease (EVD) transmission. The bishop, Mgr Sosthène Ayikuli, cited ongoing spread with confirmed cases and deaths and a lack of reliable information from officials, explaining the decision aims to prevent mass pilgrim movement from across the diocese and beyond. After consultations, he called the measure grave yet responsible and urged faithful to prepare for a future edition if conditions permit. The move reflects precautionary public health action amid an active EVD outbreak in the region, though the report does not provide exact case or death counts.

Deployment of central-level rapid intervention teams to hotspot provinces began this week, starting with South Ubangi and expanding to Kongo Central, Tanganyika, and Kwango before week’s end.

article.articleHeadline: Mosquito control is failing; Chikungunya outbreak is a concern again.
article.articleSummary: Chikungunya outbreak resurges in Kerala, India, with Thiruvananthapuram and surrounding districts reporting ongoing transmission. By August 7, 2026, the state had 114 laboratory-confirmed chikungunya cases and 63 suspected cases, plus one death. Official surveillance is judged by public health experts to underestimate true infections since chikungunya is rarely fatal and many patients are not hospitalized or tested. With rising cases amid monsoon-related warmth, Aedes mosquitoes proliferate, potentially fueling both chikungunya and dengue spread. Chikungunya reached Kerala during 2006-07 after originating in the 2004-05 Indian Ocean outbreaks, with recent years seeing renewed activity after a lull; prior reports occurred in 2019-20. High-risk groups include pregnant women, newborns, and individuals with diabetes or hypertension, who may suffer severe illness such as arthritis-like swelling, intense pain, and prolonged debility. The article provides no details on imported or exported cases. WHO had warned in July 2025 of a global resurgence risk.

article.articleHeadline: Mumbai: BMC Employee Dies After Fall During Dengue Breeding Site Inspection
article.articleSummary: 47-year-old Pandurang Todkar, a BMC Pest Control Operation Department worker, died after falling 5–7 feet while inspecting a suspected dengue breeding site at BDD Chawl No. 6-A, Bhoiwada, central Mumbai, around 3 pm. He was taken to King Edward Memorial Hospital and pronounced dead on arrival. Mayor Ritu Tawde visited the hospital, offered condolences, and directed pension and an eligible heir’s municipal job. The incident comes as Mumbai records a July 2026 surge in monsoon diseases: malaria up from 655 in June to 1,380 in July; dengue 266 to 466; gastroenteritis 603 to 851; Covid-19 27 to 58. The BMC’s citywide survey through July 26 screened 6,51,336 houses, 23,09,842 residents, collected 75,650 blood samples, and organized 123 health camps, with 52,286 leptospirosis preventive treatments. Citizens urged to take precautions against mosquito- and water-borne diseases.

article.articleHeadline: Severe dengue fever outbreak in Churnikkara | Severe dengue fever outbreak in Churnikkara
article.articleSummary: Severe dengue fever outbreak continues in Churnikkara panchayat, Kerala, with infection spreading across various areas and numerous residents under treatment. Health Inspector Arun Ghosh of Aluva filed a case in the Aluva First Class Judicial Court against the center and its owner; Junior Health Inspector K.A. Shabna had issued notices, which were not complied with. The case, under the Kerala Public Health Act 2023, carries penalties up to Rs 10,000. Rainwater accumulation at such sites fosters widespread mosquito proliferation, raising public health concerns. The Medical Officer, the local public health authority, said inspections and stringent legal action will continue against these operations and individuals to curb the outbreak.

article.articleHeadline: H5N1 Bird flu lockdown in Australia: Victoria state orders urgent warning as deadly virus spreads rapidly - Is India at risk too?
article.articleSummary: As of 9 August 2026, Victoria, Australia, has ordered a mandatory poultry lockdown as detections of H5N1 bird flu rise among birds. Agriculture Minister Julie Collins warned Australians to expect more spread and larger numbers of wildlife affected. H5N1 can infect humans who have contact with infected animals, though human cases remain small and risk is considered low; mutations may enable the virus to evade the human immune system and trigger serious symptoms. The virus is enzootic and panzootic, having killed hundreds of millions of birds and mammals worldwide, with poultry losses and spillover to cattle in United States, plus carcasses on beaches. In India, threat is high due to extensive poultry farming; since 2006, 284 H5N1 cases have been reported, with Maharashtra, West Bengal, Odisha affected, but only two human cases so far. Symptoms range from flu-like illness to severe respiratory failure; progress to ARDS, sepsis, or multi-organ failure is possible.

article.articleHeadline: Yellow fever, spread by mosquito bites in Africa, kills thousands every year! Could this deadly disease reach India as well?
article.articleSummary: Yellow fever is a viral disease transmitted by Aedes, Haemagogus, and Sabethes mosquitoes, occurring primarily in Africa and parts of South and Central America. WHO estimates 67,000–173,000 severe infections annually, with 31,000–82,000 deaths, and about 50% mortality among severe cases within 7–10 days. Transmission cycles include sylvatic (jungle) spread from mosquitoes biting wild primates to humans; intermediate cycles in Africa; and urban outbreaks when infected individuals introduce the virus into densely populated areas. Incubation is typically 3–6 days, with fever, headache, back and muscle pain, reduced appetite, and nausea; some cases are mild, while others progress to jaundice, dark urine, abdominal pain, and bleeding, potentially leading to death. India has no indigenous cases, though vectors exist; travelers from affected countries require proof of yellow fever vaccination, with quarantine if the certificate is missing.

article.articleHeadline: Ginger farmers, beware of this emerging fungal disease, preventive steps
article.articleSummary: Ginger farmers across several regions report an emerging Pyricularia fungal threat causing tiny needlepoint black to olive-green spots on leaves, often with a yellow halo, progressing to leaf desiccation and rapid plant rot with substantial yield losses. The infection can spread quickly within a cultivation area if unchecked. For the upcoming season, preventive measures include targeted sprays during the third and fourth months after planting: Propiconazole at 1 ml per litre of water, or a mix of Carbendazim 25% EC and Mancozeb 63% WP at 2 g per litre. Seed treatment is crucial: select disease-free seed rhizomes, soak in the fungicide solution for 30 minutes, then thoroughly shade-dry before planting. Emphasis on healthy planting material and timely protection is essential to reduce early fungal attacks and safeguard future ginger crops.

Officials say causes are unconfirmed pending health department investigations, but contaminated drinking water, leaks in pipelines, and sanitation gaps are suspected factors. Mayor Ramu Rohara appealed to residents to boil water before consumption and announced a 1 crore rupee allocation to shut aging pipelines, while a new pipeline system is being arranged. He plans to visit identified locations today to assess the situation.

article.articleHeadline: Rising malaria outbreak in Surguja: 74 patients detected, health department on alert, infection affecting the hill regions.
article.articleSummary: As of 9 August 2026, Surguja district, Chhattisgarh, faces a malaria outbreak with 74 confirmed cases reported from Lunda and Udaipur areas, spanning several villages in Lunda, Lakhnpur, and Udaipur, including hill-region localities such as Mataringa, Kharranagar, and Musar-dand. Health authorities are on alert, conducting door-to-door screening using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), identifying suspected and positive cases, and providing treatment per protocol. Delays are attributed to treatment by quacks, hindering early reporting. Positive cases receive immediate therapy, while communities are advised to prevent mosquito breeding around homes and seek prompt testing for fever. The focus is rapid case identification, timely treatment, and interrupting transmission chains in these affected mountainous areas.

article.articleHeadline: Skin infections, fever top health complaints in flood-hit Upper Assam, 50 doctors deployed
article.articleSummary: Amid floods in Upper Assam, a 50-member medical team has been deployed to deliver care and curb disease spread. Fifteen doctors are currently treating patients at Alengmora (West Jorhat), Teok and Kamarbandha (Golaghat); from tomorrow the full 50-member contingent will move to Sivasagar and Charaideo for three days. Over 1,000 people were seen at health camps on Sunday. Clinicians report skin infections and itching as the most common complaints, with additional cases of fever, gastric problems and mental stress. The 50 doctors come from Nagaon, Lakhimpur, Nalbari and Guwahati, with personnel from Gauhati Medical College and Hospital. The drive is part of a broader response involving more than 200 doctors and paramedics to prevent outbreaks. No major disease outbreak has been reported yet; dermatologists are treating skin infections.

article.articleHeadline: Beware of Typhoid and Food Poisoning from Eating Outside in the Rain.
article.articleSummary: Typhoid fever and food poisoning risk surge during the monsoon in Rishikesh, India, due to contaminated food and water from street vendors. Street foods such as golgappes, chaat, samosas, and pakoras are often prepared with water stored in open containers; rain, moisture, flies, and dust heighten bacterial contamination, while repeated reuse of frying oil can compromise quality. Foods left uncovered or prepared with dirty ingredients pose infection risks. Food poisoning can cause vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and weakness; typhoid is linked to contaminated food/water during the monsoon. Preventive measures include drinking clean, boiled or filtered water, thoroughly washing fruits and vegetables, and avoiding keeping cooked foods at room temperature. Vulnerable groups (children, elderly, immunocompromised) are at greater risk.

article.articleHeadline: Measles-Rubella (MR) patients still being found after vaccination, medical professionals shocked — Bulandshahr sees MR cases despite Measles-Rubella vaccination.
article.articleSummary: Bulandshahr, Uttar Pradesh, India: Measles-Rubella (MR) vaccination campaigns are underway, but MR cases continue to appear. According to WHO, 40 MR cases were reported in the six months from January 1 to June 30, with six samples sent for laboratory testing. The 40 patients this year range from 4 months to 22 years old. Reasons include not receiving both vaccine doses, waning immunity, or high virus transmission. District Immunization Officer Dr. Shashikant Rai notes vaccination reduces severity and stresses completing both doses, as some children receive only the first dose. Previously, MR vaccination covered 134,369 children across 2,581 schools. A diphtheria campaign has been running since August 3, targeting 47,866 children, while an MR vaccination drive for about 48,877 children is planned in the upcoming campaign.

article.articleHeadline: Ziro/Santé: the province stands up against malaria through the National Vector Control Days.
article.articleSummary: Malaria remains a major public health issue in Burkina Faso; the Ziro province launched the National Vector Control Days in Kation, Sapouy, to contribute to malaria elimination by 2030. Led by High Commissioner Saïba Zoromé, the event mobilized administrative, paramilitary, traditional and religious authorities, civil society, and a highly engaged population. Zoromé urged households to adopt hygiene and environmental sanitation, destroy mosquito breeding sites, and eliminate standing water. Emphasis was placed on proper use of long-lasting impregnated mosquito nets, housing sanitation, and active community participation in vector-control campaigns. In a symbolic act, the delegation visited several concessions in Kation, identifying and destroying larval habitats, underscoring the campaign’s dual educational-operational approach. Health authorities state that fighting malaria requires community commitment; all communes, villages and concessions are urged to destroy larval habitats and maintain a clean environment, aligning with the 2030 national elimination goal.

article.articleHeadline: The rain has paused, viral fever patients on the rise in the city.
article.articleSummary: Viral infections with fever, along with cold and cough, are rising in Ahmedabad, India, as the rain pauses and humidity increases. Experts report a 20–30% rise in viral fever cases over the last four days. At Ahmedabad Civil Hospital, July saw 574 adult viral infections; in the first eight days of August, 153 adults presented with viral illness. Pediatric numbers show a similar upward trend: 79 cases in June, 116 in July, and 39 children admitted in the first eight days of August. Most affected are young children and the elderly. article.articleHeadline: Leptospirosis cases surge nearly 125-fold in Telangana in two years
article.articleSummary: Telangana saw leptospirosis infections rise from 2 in 2023 to 249 in 2025, with 101 confirmed cases by June 2026, signaling ongoing monsoon transmission per Rajya Sabha data on surveillance of monsoon-related diseases. Across India, Kerala reported 4,001 cases in 2025, followed by Tamil Nadu (2,862), Karnataka (2,302) and Maharashtra (2,184); Telangana exhibited the sharpest proportional rise, while Ladakh and Lakshadweep reported negligible cases. Leptospirosis is a bacterial disease transmitted via water/soil contaminated with urine from infected animals, especially rodents; outbreaks correlate with heavy rains and flooding. In Hyderabad, clinicians note 10–15 cases monthly. A recent private hospital case: a 27-year-old man with high fever, severe myalgia, and worsening kidney function after floodwater exposure, laboratory-confirmed leptospirosis; treated with antibiotics and kidney-supportive care, recovered without dialysis. Early diagnosis and prompt antibiotics are crucial to prevent kidney, liver, lung, or brain complications; preventive measures include avoiding floodwater, footwear, gloves, wound care.

article.articleHeadline: Pushing One Health approach, U.P. priorities early identification and reporting of emerging zoonotic diseases
article.articleSummary: As of 10 August 2026, Uttar Pradesh's Animal Husbandry Department, under the RISE Global Health Security (RISE GHS) Project, is expanding early identification and reporting of emerging zoonotic diseases through strengthened One Health surveillance. Active surveillance for Avian Influenza among wild migratory birds was conducted at 19 Ramsar and other important wetland sites across the state. In the previous migratory season, over 1,100 samples were collected and tested at IVRI, Bareilly, with plans to repeat surveillance across all Ramsar sites during the upcoming migratory period. Initiatives include a Compendium for Veterinarians on Zoonotic & Priority Animal Diseases, ELISA-based testing for priority zoonoses, and farm-level biosecurity improvements in Pilibhit and Gorakhpur. A State-Level Training of Trainers for government veterinarians will strengthen interdepartmental coordination, data sharing, outbreak response, and broader One Health surveillance in collaboration with Forest and Wildlife Department.

article.articleHeadline: How drug-resistant TB evades detection in standard tests
article.articleSummary: Rifampicin-resistant TB is not reliably detected by standard tests that screen only the 81-base-pair RRDR of rpoB. Non-RRDR mutations outside RRDR cause resistance, enabling ineffective treatment and ongoing transmission. A review by IIT-Guwahati and IIT-Madras cites non-RRDR mutations in North-East India, Eswatini, Myanmar, Peru, and South Africa; in Eswatini, about 30% of drug-resistant TB cases carried such mutations missed by routine tests. Resistance can arise from changes to rifampicin binding or from co-occurring mutations that boost bacterial fitness. Moving beyond RRDR, whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) detect broader resistance; Deeplex Myc-TB has identified V170F and I491F mutations in sputum and stool. In rural labs, MAS-PCR and HRMA offer faster, cheaper alternatives, while nanopore sequencing promises portable, real-time detection. For high-burden countries like India, adopting non-RRDR diagnostics is essential to halt silent spread.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue fever; fear has not subsided in the stomach and chest region.
article.articleSummary: As of 10 August 2026, dengue fever fears persist in Mathathumbhagam, Eranjoli panchayat, Talassery. A housewife was the first patient; after recovery, her husband fell ill, and six people in Mathathumbhagam have been reported with dengue. Although some patients recovered, community anxiety remains. Vector-control efforts, including Kudumbashree volunteers and health workers, have begun to eliminate dengue sources, but awareness is still limited. Earlier dengue cases had been reported in nearby areas such as Vadakkumbad and Vaathilpeedik. Confirmed dengue cases occurred in June and July. Mosquitoes breed where stagnant water accumulates, including in vessels and containers near homes. Despite monsoon-cleanup efforts to clear roads and drains, water-filled vessels persist. Health workers are conducting home visits; ward sanitation committee meetings chaired by the medical officer have urged continued household cleanliness and community education.

article.articleHeadline: 'Flesh-Eating' Bacteria In US Beaches: Could Vibrio Infection Be A Risk In India Too? What To Know
article.articleSummary: Vibrio vulnificus, a bacterium thriving in warm seawater and brackish water, can infect people through cuts or wounds or by eating raw shellfish, potentially causing severe wound infections or bloodstream infections. In the United States, a rise in coastal-water connected infections prompts warnings; Louisiana has recorded nine infections this year, all hospitalized, with five deaths. Symptoms after coastal exposure include increasing redness, swelling, warmth, severe pain or discoloration around a wound, fever and chills; severe cases can blister the skin or cause rapid tissue damage. Most infections are uncommon, but risk remains for open wounds exposed to coastal waters and for consuming raw oysters. The article notes India could face exposure but does not report an outbreak; guidance emphasizes cleaning wounds, proper cooking of seafood, and not panicking about beaches.

Department Circular No. 39 bans entry of live swine, cattle, water buffaloes, and other susceptible species, plus fresh skeletal muscle meat, animal casings, tallow, hooves, horns, and bovine semen. Safe commodities may enter with sanitary certifications; allowed items include ultra-high-temperature milk, dairy products, heat-treated canned meat, protein meal, gelatin, and processed hides and leather. FAO-confirmed localized SAT1 FMD outbreaks were verified by WOAH labs. Border quarantine officers will intercept non-compliant shipments. FMD affects cloven-hoofed animals and poses no human health risk but can devastate livestock production and farmer livelihoods. Imports largely come from Brazil, the US, and Spain.

article.articleHeadline: Consultant for Al-Youm: Wolbachia technology reduces mosquitoes' ability to transmit dengue and Zika.
article.articleSummary: As of 9 August 2026, Dr. Ashwaq Al-Nazawi, a Saudi public health specialist and vector-borne disease expert, participated as the Kingdom’s representative in the Brazil Learning Exchange 2026 organized by the World Mosquito Program (Monash University) in Curitiba, Brazil. The program centers on Wolbachia, a natural bacterium used to reduce Aedes aegypti’s capacity to transmit dengue, Zika, and chikungunya. It featured lectures, workshops, field visits, and demonstrations of Brazil’s large-scale production of Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes, quality assurance, operational readiness, release, and community monitoring. Al-Nazawi met World Mosquito Program founder Prof. Scott O’Neill and engaged with Brazilian officials and the Curitiba mayor to exchange best practices, discuss challenges, and explore international partnerships with WHO and the US CDC. The initiative emphasizes sustainability, community involvement, funding, and strategic planning to bolster Saudi Arabia’s vector-control and public-health efforts in line with Vision 2030.

article.articleHeadline: The veterinarian warns that the vaccine is the only protection against rabies.
article.articleSummary: Rabies is a viral zoonosis causing fatal CNS disease in mammals, including humans, with nearly 100% mortality once clinical signs appear. Transmission occurs mainly through bite saliva; after entry the virus travels via nerves to the CNS and salivary glands. Bats are the primary reservoirs in Brazil, but foxes, wild canids, and primates can also harbor the virus. Domestic dogs and cats experience rare cases. Diagnosis is definitive post-mortem via CNS tissue; ante-mortem suspicion relies on clinical signs, exposure history, and RT-PCR on saliva or CSF, though negative results do not rule out infection. Because rabies is a notifiable disease and a major public health concern, exposed individuals should seek immediate medical evaluation for post-exposure prophylaxis. Vaccination remains the cornerstone of prevention; Cuiabá conducts free canine/feline vaccination campaigns; avoid contact with bats and report abnormal wildlife, ensuring timely veterinary and public health action.

article.articleHeadline: Meet the Virus That Could Affect the Fetal Brain
article.articleSummary: Oropouche virus, described in 1955, circulates mainly in the Amazon, causing febrile illness indistinguishable from dengue, Zika, and chikungunya. From 2024 Brazil recorded the largest expansion, with about 14,000 confirmed cases in 2024 and high levels in 2025. Infected pregnant women have reported vertical transmission and fetal outcomes including abortions, fetal death, microcephaly, and congenital malformations. To understand fetal brain infection, researchers used human brain organoids (mini-brains). They compared two strains: BeAn1991 from the Amazon in 1960, and RJ/LVM-2024 from the Rio de Janeiro epidemic with a rearrangement. Both infected neural stem cells; BeAn1991 infected ~87% of exposed cells, RJ/LVM-2024 slightly less, with complete replication cycles. Transcriptomics found 657 differentially expressed genes, with reduced neural progenitor proliferation and upregulated inflammatory, replication, and cell-death pathways. In organoids around 30 days, infection impaired growth and disrupted structure, especially in ventricular zones; Ki67 declined, signaling slowed brain development.

article.articleHeadline: Very strong El Niño raises public health alert in Brazilian livestock farming.
article.articleSummary: Strong El Niño in Brazil raises livestock biosecurity concerns. Official forecasts from MCTI, based on CPC/NOAA, indicate an 81% probability that El Niño will reach a very strong phase between October and December 2026, possibly persisting into early 2027. In the South region, rainfall is expected above average, while the central-north may face below-normal rainfall and higher temperatures, complicating herd management nationwide. Prolonged rains can create mud and standing water in facilities, hindering sanitation and promoting persistence of infectious agents; heat and water scarcity raise animal stress, affecting welfare and handling. Consequently, emphasis on biosafety measures, facility cleaning, restricted animal movement, and vehicle disinfection becomes critical to reduce between-farm transmission. Truck transport between properties, auctions, and processing units poses a risk due to organic matter on vehicles, especially during heavy rains. Regional impacts vary; continuous meteorological and hydrological monitoring is advised through the coming months.

article.articleHeadline: Outbreak of gastrointestinal illness linked to contaminated lettuce raises alarm; see symptoms and how to protect yourself.
article.articleSummary: Cyclospora cayetanensis infection (cyclosporiasis) linked to contaminated romaine lettuce has sickened people in 15 U.S. states, with exposure tied to Taco Bell restaurants and lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms of Mexico. Symptoms typically appear days after ingestion and can last weeks without treatment, including severe diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea, loss of appetite, fatigue, dehydration, and sometimes low fever. Higher risk for elderly, children, and immunocompromised. Transmission occurs via contaminated food or water; washing produce helps but may not fully eliminate parasite if contaminated. Public health officials are monitoring the outbreak and updating case counts as investigations conclude; remains centered in the United States with no export of cases reported.

article.articleSummary: São Carlos, Brazil, begins installing 220 ovitraps in homes and businesses to monitor Aedes aegypti and arboviral diseases, including Dengue, Zika, and Chikungunya. Ovitraps attract gravid females to lay eggs; collected paddles are sent to the Unidade de Controle de Zoonoses e Endemias laboratory for egg counting, enabling targeted vector control. Installations occur in high-risk areas at up to 150 cm height, shielded from rain and sun and kept away from children and pets. The 5‑day cycle deploys on Thursdays–Fridays and collects on Mondays–Tuesdays. Residents volunteered to participate. As of 2026, São Carlos has 404 confirmed Dengue cases with no deaths; 171 Chikungunya, 154 Zika, and 1 Yellow Fever cases have been ruled out. Data will guide surveillance and preventive actions to reduce urban arbovirus transmission.

article.articleHeadline: High Risks in Cross-Border Medical Aesthetics (3-2): Infection, Necrosis, Illegal Fillers — Doctors Reveal the Risks
article.articleSummary: Taipei plastic surgeons warn that cross-border cosmetic procedures pose serious post-operative risks for patients returning from China or Korea. Infections and vascular embolism causing tissue necrosis are common complications when follow-up care is limited after overseas treatments, and unapproved fillers used abroad can migrate and trigger chronic inflammation. Post-operative care is the main challenge: brief overseas stays hinder ongoing monitoring, leaving Taiwanese physicians without complete medical records and raising repair difficulty. Materials used overseas differ from Taiwan regulations; some Chinese clinics reportedly use unnamed 'Ukrainian gel' for breast and buttock augmentation, which may migrate; Korea’s exosome and stem cell therapies can produce facial irregularities requiring home-based treatment. Documented cases include nasal ala necrosis from vascular embolism after hyaluronic acid in Korea, leg infections after overseas fillers, and an umbilical deformity after abdominal lift in China. Travel after surgery also increases infection, thrombosis, and slower recovery; thorough pre-op evaluation and long-term post-care plans are essential.

article.articleHeadline: Bird flu is here, and Australia's vulnerable wildlife is unprepared for it
article.articleSummary: As of 9 August 2026, H5 bird flu has reached mainland Australia after ~30 years of spread from southern China, first impacting Heard Island’s seabird and elephant seal colonies in the Southern Ocean, where it killed about three-quarters of elephant seal pups and then crossed over 4,000 kilometres to the mainland. Globally, the virus has affected around 600 bird species and 100 mammal species, wiping out millions of wild birds and tens of thousands of mammals; many hosts are immunologically naive. The pathogen is a compact, rapidly mutating entity with ten proteins and eight RNA segments; once established in wildlife, it cannot be eliminated or treated. Response centers on boosting wildlife resilience by mitigating other threats—habitat loss, invasive species, fires, degraded water—rather than cures. Advocates urge $200 million over two years for wildlife resilience, about $13 per taxpayer, leveraging the Disaster Ready Fund, and caution against parrot imports that could introduce new pathogens.

article.articleHeadline: These seemingly safe behaviors still carry a risk of HIV infection—have you fallen into the trap?
article.articleSummary: HIV/AIDS remains a significant risk in China, especially among men who have sex with men (MSM), with 7–8% infection in MSM and over 80% of new infections among youth students attributed to MSM activity. Misconceptions persist: unprotected oral sex carries nonzero risk (about 0–0.04% per act in Zhejiang data) and can transmit HIV when oral ulcers or mucosal breaks exist; it also facilitates other STIs that raise HIV risk. Anal intercourse carries higher per-exposure risk: receptive anal sex about 1.38%, insertive about 0.11%, with risk for both without condoms. Transmission can occur via rectal mucosa and high-risk fluids such as semen and prostate fluid, even without ejaculation. Relationships do not guarantee safety; fixed partners can be infected, so testing is essential. After high-risk exposure, PEP should be sought within 72 hours for 28 days; but consistent condom use and regular testing remain the best preventive measures.

article.articleHeadline: One scientist's 1933 rat lungworm discovery opened the door to understanding a public health threat
article.articleSummary: Angiostrongylus cantonensis (rat lungworm) was first described in 1933 in Guangzhou by H.T. Chen. The parasite cycles through rats, slugs and snails; humans ingest larvae via contaminated produce (notably lettuce) or undercooked intermediate hosts (freshwater prawns, frogs, crayfish, crabs, and some freshwater fish). In humans, larvae can reach the central nervous system, causing symptoms from headache, fever, fatigue, neck pain, numbness, and photophobia to meningitis, paralysis, coma, disability, or death. The parasite has spread beyond its origin to Southeast Asia, Australia, Latin America, and several U.S. areas, including Hawai'i, Florida, and the Gulf Coast. Roughly 7,000 global cases have been reported, about 10 per year in the U.S., mostly in Hawai'i. Diagnosis involves blood tests and meningitis evaluation; prevention emphasizes washing produce, cooking seafood and freshwater hosts to 165°F, and limiting snail/slug exposure in homes and with pets.

The spread is not strictly seasonal, though winter indoor crowding historically increases transmission; with windows closed and air conditioning on, transmission differences are minimal. Large gatherings such as Hajj can involve attendees from many countries, potentially introducing influenza and COVID into other regions depending on season. China remains prone to infectious disease outbreaks due to its large population, though the exact current pathogen is unknown; novel viruses can emerge from wildlife, domestic animals, or poultry, especially where human-animal contact is high, and local dietary practices may influence transmission in some areas.

article.articleHeadline: Avian Influenza: Developments Raise Concerns Among European Livestock Farmers.
article.articleSummary: H5N1 avian influenza spreading among U.S. dairy cattle raises alarm in Europe. German experiments show European genotypes can readily infect dairy cows; the virus is well established among Europe’s wild birds and repeatedly affects poultry. The dominant H5N1 lineage originated in China in 1996 (domestic geese) and spread via wild birds to Europe, Africa and the Americas. From December 2025 to February 2026, almost 16 million poultry were culled or died on infected European farms; by June 2026, a further six million birds were affected. Transmission routes include contact with wild waterfowl and contamination from vehicle wheels and footwear. Cattle are under surveillance; Norway reported May deaths of a polar bear and a walrus on Svalbard; an Alaska polar bear died in 2023. EFSA says the risk of the U.S. genotype reaching Europe is very low, though antibodies were found in Dutch dairy cows; the EU is examining expanded vaccination.

article.articleHeadline: Rabies Detected in a Ferret-Badger in 2013 by the Institute of Veterinary Medicine; Not Imported from Abroad — The Virus May Have Existed in Taiwan's Wildlife for Over a Century, Forming an Independently Evolving Endemic Lineage.
article.articleSummary: Rabies in Taiwan: A 2013 wild ferret-badger case (Institute of Veterinary Medicine) is not imported, indicating an endemic wildlife lineage. As of 2026-08-10, mathematical modeling and retrospective sequencing suggest the virus has circulated in native wildlife for over a century, forming an independently evolving local lineage within the SEA-5 Asian lineage, distinct from strains in China, Korea, and Southeast Asia. Domestic vaccination has prevented dog-cat transmission cycles, and Taiwan has moved away from the non-epidemic status after reporting the 2013 case to the OIE. Retrospective samples show positivity as early as 2010, with traces back to 2004, underscoring tracing challenges due to limited preserved material. Wildlife cases persist, with western spread across the Da’an River into Nanzhuang, Miaoli, and eastern spread across Mugua Creek toward Hualien City, highlighting ongoing wildlife transmission despite vaccination efforts.

article.articleHeadline: Chongqing Infectious Disease Expert Liu Min Reminds: Monkeypox Is Nearby; If You Suspect Infection, Where Should You Seek Treatment?
article.articleSummary: Monkeypox is no longer an 'African disease' in China. Mainland China’s first imported case was detected in Chongqing in September 2022, with a local outbreak in August 2024. From 2023–2026 monthly reports show ongoing cases: January 28, March 28, April 32, May 86; most locally acquired belong to lineage IIb; no deaths reported. Transmission is via close skin-to-skin contact and sexual contact, with men who have sex with men and HIV-positive individuals disproportionately affected (over 40%). Incubation is 5–21 days (commonly 6–13). Signs include fever ≥38.5°C, lymphadenopathy, and a vesiculopustular rash beginning on the face/oral region and possibly involving genitals/anal area, lasting 2–4 weeks. Diagnosis relies on PCR from lesion samples; rapid testing is available at Chongqing Public Health Medical Rescue Center. No domestically approved vaccine yet; vaccines exist in Hong Kong, Macau, and Thailand; a Chinese mRNA vaccine entered US/China trials in 2026. Prevention emphasizes avoiding close skin contact and high-risk sexual behavior; most patients recover with supportive care; seek Infectious Diseases Department care promptly.

article.articleHeadline: Large-scale outbreak of parasitic diseases in the United States; several key tips to confidently enjoy fruits and vegetables (photo gallery)
article.articleSummary: As of July 23, 2026, the United States reports what CDC calls the largest cyclosporiasis outbreak in recent years, with several deaths and ongoing investigations. Some clusters may be linked to a Taco Bell lettuce supplier, but the infection source remains unconfirmed and not all cases are from a single supply chain. Cyclosporiasis is caused by Cyclospora cayetanensis (and related Cryptosporidium parasites) and is acquired mainly through consuming food or water contaminated with feces—especially unwashed lettuce, fresh berries, and herbs. Incubation is 2–14 days; symptoms include persistent watery diarrhea, severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, dehydration, and fatigue. Antimicrobial treatment is effective; fatalities are rare. Prevention emphasizes soap-and-water handwashing (not alcohol sanitizers), thorough produce washing, removing outer leaves, peeling or cooking implicated items, and strict kitchen hygiene. Travelers to the U.S. and parts of Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia) should avoid raw lettuce, use boiled water, and seek prompt care if diarrhea persists, with travel history noted.

article.articleHeadline: Which infectious diseases are most likely to break out in schools?
article.articleSummary: Measles, varicella (chickenpox), hand‑foot‑and‑mouth disease (HFMD) and seasonal influenza are highlighted as highly transmissible in schools. Measles spreads mainly through airborne droplets and can be transmitted from about 4 days before to 4 days after rash; symptoms include fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and a spreading rash. Varicella spreads via respiratory droplets and direct contact with vesicle fluid and is contagious 1–2 days before rash until all lesions crust; fever, fatigue and itchy vesicular rash are common. HFMD, often due to EV71, affects young children and presents with fever, oral ulcers and hand/foot rashes; transmission is fecal–oral, saliva, respiratory secretions, and contaminated objects, with prolonged contagiousness after symptoms ease. Seasonal flu transmits by droplets in crowded, enclosed spaces; vaccination is recommended yearly. Vietnam uses EV71 vaccine for HFMD but vaccines don’t cover all enteroviruses. Schools should emphasize cleaning, ventilation, surface disinfection, and rapid isolation of cases.

From August 1, 2026, fines for releasing dogs in public without a muzzle, leash, or handler rise from 600,000–800,000 VND to 1–2 million. Vietnam sees over 400,000 prophylaxis treatments annually after bites; 2025 rabies deaths totaled 80 nationwide. Emphasis on education and prompt medical care after exposure is stressed.

article.articleHeadline: Personal hygiene: Simple habits help prevent many infectious diseases.
article.articleSummary: Personal hygiene is highlighted as a simple yet crucial measure to reduce the spread of infectious diseases in Vietnam. To interrupt transmission, the article notes three components: source, route, and susceptible hosts, with hands as the main conduit. Regular handwashing with soap under running water for at least 30 seconds removes most pathogens responsible for diarrhea and respiratory infections, and routine cleaning of frequently touched surfaces is advised. It emphasizes preserving natural barriers through oral/nasal hygiene (daily saline rinses) and skin care, plus bathing to prevent secondary infections. Community responsibility is stressed: covering coughs/sneezes, disposing of tissues, and washing hands afterward. Five daily habits include handwashing at key times, not sharing personal items, clean clothing, environmental cleaning, and respiratory hygiene. Dengue, spread by Aedes mosquitoes, requires bite avoidance and vector control, while vaccination against measles, chickenpox, and influenza complements hygiene. Article by Dr. Nguyen Minh Hien, Hanoi.

article.articleHeadline: Protecting children from the risk of disease outbreaks in the new school year.
article.articleSummary: To prevent school-year infectious outbreaks, experts at the National University Hospital Hanoi urge parents to complete routine immunizations at least two weeks before students return to class. Returning students increase exposure to pathogens via droplets and shared surfaces; younger children often have lower hygiene. Vaccines emphasized include respiratory protection: seasonal influenza, pneumococcus, measles, and pertussis; vaccines to prevent diarrhea; and vaccines for serious diseases such as Japanese encephalitis and meningococcal disease. HPV and meningococcal vaccines are advised for preteens aged 9–14. The Hanoi hospital system imports vaccines through official channels, maintains strict cold-chain storage, and observes 30 minutes post-vaccination. Parents can book via Facebook to check vaccination history and receive reminders. This strengthens community immunity ahead of school openings as of 9 August 2026.

article.articleHeadline: West Nile virus gains strength in Greece: 65 cases, 6 deaths, Attica in a high-risk zone.

Twenty patients remain hospitalized, eight in ICU. Attica accounts for most activity, especially eastern Attica: Spata-Artemida (11 cases, 10 neuroinvasive), Markopoulo-Mesogesia (7), Pallini (5); cases also in Acharnes, Vari-Voula-Vouliagmeni, Koropi, Lavrio, Marathon, Peania, Rafina-Pikermi, Aghia Paraskevi, Nea Ionia, Papagou-Holargos, Halandri, Glyfada, and several Athens municipalities. Outside Attica, cases detected in Thessaly and Central Macedonia (Karditsa, Larissa, Trikala, Pella, Serres; Palamas, Tempi, Nea Zichni). article.articleHeadline: Contagion
article.articleSummary: Chickenpox (varicella) outbreaks in a school prompted rapid containment: several students affected; administrator shifted to online classes, sent symptomatic children home, disinfected facilities, and created a line list of attendees with full varicella vaccination or history of infection. Varicella is highly communicable, spread by direct contact and airborne routes, and can be contagious two days before symptoms; secondary cases may be more severe, risking immunocompromised students. Most parents lacked varicella immunization; advice urged vaccination as soon as possible and home observation, with medical clearance required before return for recovered cases. The article notes gaps in booster availability beyond the national immunization program and cost barriers for some families. It highlights schools as sites for transmission of rhinovirus and vaccine-preventable diseases, and notes dengue and chikungunya risk in dengue-endemic countries; notifiable dengue warrants outbreak investigations. Preventive measures include hand hygiene, cough etiquette, staying home when ill, and adequate ventilation.

article.articleHeadline: Palace urges vigilance vs leptospirosis, orders DOH to be proactive
article.articleSummary: Philippines, August 10, 2026: Widespread flooding in Metro Manila and other regions driven by the enhanced southwest monsoon (habagat) prompts vigilance against leptospirosis. Malacañang says President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. has directed the Department of Health to take proactive measures against illnesses tied to prolonged rainfall and flooding. Exposed individuals should wash with clean water and soap and seek medical consultation at health centers. Free consultation and doxycycline are available at health centers, though doxycycline is not recommended for pregnant women and children 12 and under without medical assessment. The DOH has established Dengue Fast Lanes in hospitals to facilitate treatment for dengue suspects. Authorities are preparing clean-water containers (jerry cans) and chlorine tablets to ensure safe drinking water. Boil water for two minutes after it reaches a rolling boil. Do not wait for fever, jaundice, or decreased urine output before seeking medical attention for possible leptospirosis.

article.articleHeadline: Wild monkeys 'go berserk' attack 18 people, dozens of schools in Indonesia forced to close.
article.articleSummary: On Sumatra island, Indonesia, an adult long-tailed macaque attacked 18 residents in Tembilahan, with 19 total attacks and one person hit twice, causing injuries that required stitches and rabies vaccination. The macaque was trapped on Aug 6 and later moved to Pekanbaru, Riau province, where authorities will conduct blood tests to detect any infectious pathogens. In response, about 40 local schools were closed on Aug 7, forcing hundreds of students in Tembilahan to study online for three days; reopening is planned for Aug 10 if safe. Officials warn the animal could trigger further attacks if others in the wild form groups. The incident underscores human–wildlife conflict linked to deforestation for palm oil, which reduces primate habitat and may push monkeys to rely on human food or be abandoned pets.
